name: Daria Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on Ward 7, which is orthopaedics at the city hospital, so mostly hip and knee replacements and older people who've had a fall. A day shift starts at seven with handover, then it's obs, pain scores, wound checks and getting people up on their new joints with the physios. I like the moment someone walks to the window on day two after a new knee. What wears me out is the paperwork and the phone, because every discharge seems to need three calls to the care home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been on that ward, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Five years now, since I qualified, so I'm one of the steady middle people the newer nurses ask. I live with my partner Julien, who's a mechanic at the bus depot, in a rented flat about twenty minutes away. We've got roughly four months of bills put by, which feels okay but not like a lot. We're talking about buying somewhere in the next couple of years, if prices let us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at handover: good, now can the computer please do the discharge letters. Nursing isn't going anywhere, people still need someone to turn them and check their wounds. I wouldn't post about it, I'm not really an online person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means my job stays as it is, which is mostly fine but also means the hard bits stay. We're short two nurses on most shifts and that won't fix itself because a computer got a bit better. The thing on my mind is rent going up again and whether Julien and I ever manage a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and put my name down for the tissue viability course the ward lead keeps mentioning, because that's a pay step. I'd try whatever note-writing tool the trust brings in, once the others say it actually saves time. And I'd keep putting about two hundred a month into the house fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly normal, a bit tired. It's not frightening, it's just the same squeeze we're already in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the hard bits stay. What's the hardest bit right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Short staffing. Last Tuesday I had eight patients and two of them were confused at night and kept trying to climb out of bed. A smarter computer doesn't hold someone's hand at three in the morning, and nobody's paying for an extra nurse either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the routine stuff did get automated, which part of your day would you actually hand over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The discharge summaries and chasing beds, without thinking twice. On Ward 7 the slowest part of any discharge is the paperwork, not the patient. If the computer did that, I'd get maybe forty minutes a shift back for actual nursing.

say: I'd tell colleagues **nursing stays human**, and the computer can take the discharge letters.
I'd keep it to work chat, because I'm **not online** much and don't post opinions.
think: Privately I think my job is **safe**, but the **short staffing** on Ward 7 stays.
The real worry is **rent** rising and whether we ever save a **house deposit**.
do: Sign up for the **tissue viability** course this year because it leads to a **pay step**.
Try the trust's **note-writing tool** once colleagues say it really saves time.
Keep paying about **200 a month** into the house fund with Julien.
feel: She feels **tired** but not frightened, because it's the **same squeeze** she already lives with.
S0.quote: A smarter computer doesn't hold someone's hand at three in the morning, and nobody's paying for an extra nurse either.
fieldNote: Her worry here isn't AI at all; it's **staffing** and a **thin path** to buying a home.
She'd adopt tools only after **colleagues vouch** for them, which fits her steady way of changing.
The **forty minutes** a shift she'd win back is the one concrete gain she sees.

steps.text: Keep working day shifts on the orthopaedic ward
Take the tissue viability course for the next pay step
Use the trust's note-writing tool once colleagues trust it
Put about 200 a month into the house deposit fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the clever stuff is coming for the offices first, not us. We'd probably joke that the bed managers should worry before the nurses do. With friends I'd say it's good if it takes the forms away, as long as it doesn't take the staff away too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it changes my day more than my job. The rota, the ordering, the notes, the discharge planning, a lot of that is thinking work and it'll move to software. What worries me is managers deciding that if the computer saves an hour, they can run a shift with one nurse fewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be on whatever group tests the new systems on Ward 7, because I'd rather shape it than have it dropped on us. I'd do the tissue viability course this year and maybe look at a second skill like plaster care. Money-wise I'd keep saving and not take on a car loan, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, if I'm honest. Not scared for me, but I can see the shift getting thinner around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the ward would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our ward clerk, Pauline (the ward's clerk for twenty years), runs the place in ways nobody notices. If booking and phones go to software, her job's the obvious one to cut. I'd also worry about the healthcare assistants if lifting robots ever turn up, but that feels further off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather shape it. What would you actually say in that group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say test it on a real night shift, not a quiet Tuesday morning with the managers watching. If the computer saves an hour, I'd want it written down that the hour goes back to patients, not into cutting a nurse's post. I don't know if they'd listen.

say: I'd say the change hits **offices first**, and nurses are behind the **bed managers** in line.
I'd tell friends it's fine if it removes **forms**, as long as it keeps **staff**.
think: She expects her **day** to change more than her **job**, as notes and rotas go digital.
The fear is managers using saved time to run a shift with **one nurse fewer**.
do: Volunteer for the **testing group** when new systems reach Ward 7.
Finish **tissue viability** this year and look into a **plaster care** skill next.
Hold off on a **car loan** and keep the house savings going.
feel: She's **uneasy**, safe herself but watching the **shift thin** around her.
S1.quote: If the computer saves an hour, I'd want it written down that the hour goes back to patients, not into cutting a nurse's post.
fieldNote: She separates her **own safety** from the ward's, and worries more about the **clerk** and assistants.
Her plan is to **join the testing** group, a steady person's way of getting ahead of change.
She wants a **written promise**, showing she doesn't fully trust managers' intentions.

steps.text: Join the group that tests new computer systems on Ward 7
Finish the tissue viability course and look at plaster care
Skip the car loan and keep saving for the flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say people will always need a nurse at the bedside, at least for now. I'd probably say it a bit too firmly, the way you do when you're not sure. Online I'd stay quiet, there'd be enough shouting already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think 2028 is fine for me and 2031 is the scary bit. The thinking part of nursing, like the care plans, the drug checks and the risk scores, would go to AGI almost at once. Then three years later, I'd be thirty-one with a mortgage I can't afford to lose, the year a robot can turn a patient and help them walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house hunt for a year and keep the savings as cash instead of a deposit. I'd move from tissue viability toward something more human, like the falls team or discharge liaison, where you talk families through hard choices. And I'd talk to Julien properly about whether the bus depot gets hit first, because his job is half diagnostics on a laptop already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel like I had a three-year head start but no idea which way to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Julien's job might go first. What would that mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be living on one nurse's wage, which covers the flat and food but not much else. My partner Julien would hate that, he's proud about paying his half. We'd probably have to give up the idea of buying and just rent for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in those three years between the AGI and the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever the hospital uses to run the ward, so I'm the nurse who supervises the system rather than the one it replaces. I'd keep my hands-on skills sharp, because the robots won't be perfect on day one. And I'd build up four months of savings to eight if I could.

say: I'd say firmly that people will **always need a nurse**, partly to reassure myself.
I'd keep **quiet online**, because there would be too much **shouting** already.
think: She thinks 2028 is survivable but **2031**, when **robots** arrive, is the real threat.
Care plans, **drug checks** and risk scores would go to AGI almost **at once**.
do: Pause the **house hunt** and keep the deposit as **cash** for a year.
Move toward the **falls team** or discharge liaison, where family conversations matter.
Learn the ward's **AI system** and try to double savings to **eight months**.
feel: She feels **anxious**, with a **head start** but no clear direction.
S2.quote: I'd be thirty-one with a mortgage I can't afford to lose, the year a robot can turn a patient and help them walk.
fieldNote: She reasons clearly about the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots.
The household risk is double: Julien's **diagnostic work** may go before hers.
Her instinct is to move toward **human conversations**, not toward technical roles.

steps.text: Pause the flat purchase and hold the deposit as cash
Build savings from four months of bills to eight
Apply for the falls team or a discharge liaison post
Learn the ward's AI system well enough to supervise it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so the hospital should be training people now, not later. At work I'd push for it at the staff meeting. With friends I'd say it's worrying but it's not the end of the world yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think five years gives me time to get into a role that's hard to hand to a robot. I'd be thirty-two when it reaches the bedside, and I'd want to be in something with families and judgement by then. I don't think my job disappears, but I think the ward needs fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the discharge liaison post next time it comes up, which is mostly talking to families and care homes. I'd do a short course on using the AI tools properly, because by 2031 every nurse will need it. We'd still buy a flat, but a cheaper one, so the mortgage fits on one wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, sliding into anxious when I think about 2034. It's manageable, but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would buying a cheaper flat actually mean for you and Julien?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably two bedrooms instead of three, and further out, maybe by the ring road. It'd mean a longer drive but a mortgage I could pay alone. Julien would grumble about the commute, but he's practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the ward needs fewer of you. Who decides who stays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it'd be whoever has the extra skills and isn't on a sick record, honestly. That's partly why I want the liaison role, so I'm not just one of twenty nurses who all do the same thing. It's not a nice way to think about colleagues.

say: I'd say the hospital should start **training people now**, while there are a few years.
I'd tell friends it's **worrying** but not yet the end of the world.
think: She thinks five years buys time to reach a role with **families and judgement**.
She expects the ward to keep nurses but need **fewer of them**.
do: Apply for the **discharge liaison** post when it is next advertised.
Take a short **AI tools course**, because every nurse will need it by 2031.
Buy a **cheaper flat** so the mortgage fits on **one wage**.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, edging toward **anxious** when she pictures 2034.
S3.quote: I don't think my job disappears, but I think the ward needs fewer of us.
fieldNote: She treats the five years as a **career runway**, not a reprieve.
She admits, uncomfortably, that **extra skills** decide who stays.
Planning the mortgage around **one wage** shows how real she thinks the risk is.

steps.text: Apply for the discharge liaison post at the city hospital
Take a short course on the ward's AI tools
Buy a smaller two-bedroom flat near the ring road

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent warning and we should use it. At work I'd say it's a chance to fix staffing properly before the robots arrive. Online I'd still say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like a career's worth for me. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI arrives and forty by the time robots are good at the bedside. That's time to get a master's or move into something like nurse education.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the liaison or falls role in the next couple of years, then think about a part-time master's around thirty. We'd buy the flat as planned, since a decade is long enough to pay a chunk off. I'd learn the AI tools as they come, without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly okay. It's on my mind, but it doesn't keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you study, if you did a master's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably advanced practice or teaching. I had a lecturer, Mrs Okafor (her old nursing tutor), who made the wards sound like the best job in the world. I wouldn't mind being that for someone, even if half of what I teach is how to work beside a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just that ten years is long enough for the hospital to ignore it until year nine. It took Ward 7 four years to get new beds. I'd worry the planning never happens.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a fair warning and we should **use it**.
I'd push to fix **staffing properly** before robots ever arrive.
think: She sees a decade as a **career's worth** of time to move up.
By 2039 she'd be **forty**, with time for a **master's** or teaching.
do: Move to the **liaison** or **falls** role within two years.
Start a part-time **master's** in advanced practice or teaching around thirty.
Buy the **flat as planned** and learn AI tools without rushing.
feel: She feels **fairly okay**; it's on her mind but doesn't keep her up.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for the hospital to ignore it until year nine. It took Ward 7 four years to get new beds.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her **fear into a plan**: master's, teaching or advanced practice.
Her doubt is about the **hospital's slowness**, not about her own ability.
She draws on a former **tutor** as the model for what she'd become.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's in advanced practice around age thirty
Buy the flat with Julien as originally planned
Pick up the hospital's AI tools as each one rolls out

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would land when I'm thirty-one and just starting a mortgage. What would help is the hospital telling us early which roles stay, and paying for retraining instead of leaving it to us. A bit of support for Julien too, because his job might go first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to patients. Ward 7 is full of eighty-year-olds who are scared already, and a robot lifting them out of bed would terrify some of them. I think people forget nursing is half reassurance.

headlineQuote: Ward 7 is full of eighty-year-olds who are scared already, and a robot lifting them out of bed would terrify some of them.
portrait: Daria is a **27-year-old orthopaedic nurse** on Ward 7, five years qualified, living with partner Julien.
Her real pressures are **short staffing**, rising rent and a slow path to a **house deposit**.
She stays **uneasy** in the mild pictures, worrying for the clerk and assistants more than herself.
AGI by 2028 makes her **anxious**, because robots would reach the bedside when she's thirty-one.
Longer warnings turn into **career plans**: discharge liaison, a master's or nurse education.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, since **robots** would arrive as she starts a mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: She wants the hospital to say **early** which roles stay and to **pay for retraining**.
She'd also like **support for Julien**, whose job may be hit first.
